post.description:
Grant or revoke one client for one person.

* **grant** — names the person on `sso-access-users` and lifts their own
  deny entry, which would otherwise make the grant inert. A person refused
  through a denied *group* cannot be granted here (409 `denied_by_group`).
* **revoke** — a named grant is removed; access through a group (or a
  client that restricts nobody) gets a deny entry for this person only, so
  their institution membership and everyone else's access are untouched.

Refused with 409 `state_changed` when the cell is no longer
`expected_state`, and 409 `not_applicable` when the action does not apply
to it (granting what they hold, revoking what they lack, any change to an
exempt client). Nothing is written in either case. Every change is audited
with the actor, the person, the client and both states.

The institution-scope and join-column attributes are **not** writable here —
use `PUT /client/clients/{client_id}/scope` and
`PUT /client/clients/{client_id}/join-column`. This route would accept them
happily (they are just client attributes), and that is the problem: a scope
change has a removal warning, an access cascade and an audit record, and a
join-column change has a session guard, a protocol-mapper write and an audit
record — none of which a generic attribute PUT performs. Sending one is
refused rather than silently half-applied.

get.description:
Which identifier this client authenticates users by, and what it costs.

The `join_key` claim in this client's tokens carries the value of the column
named here; the application reads that one claim and looks it up in its own
key column (`app/core/join_key.py`).

`active_sessions` is why a change is a two-step: tokens already issued keep
the *old* key until they expire, so a live client cannot be switched without
`confirm`.

`?check=true` additionally reads every user assigned to the client and
reports which of them this column would block at login — missing value,
wrong shape, or shared with another account. It is off by default because it
is a per-user read over the whole assigned population.

put.description:
Set the identifier this client uses to find its own user record.

Two things happen, and they have to happen together: the column is recorded
on the client, and the client's `sso-join-key` protocol mapper is rewritten
so its tokens actually carry that column. A recorded column whose mapper was
not written would leave the console saying one thing and the tokens saying
another — so a failed mapper write fails the request (502).

Refused with **409** when the client has active sessions and `confirm` is
not set. Their tokens keep the old key until expiry; the change is allowed,
it just may not happen silently.

The response reports which assigned users the new column would block. That
is information, not a veto — data is cleaned after the key is chosen, and
holding the change hostage to it would leave the client on the wrong key.

Every change is audited with the actor, the before and after column, the
session count and whether it was confirmed.

put.description:
Change which institutions own or may use a client. Platform admins only.

Narrowing a scope is the dangerous direction, so it is a two-step:

1. Any institution that loses the client **and has users on it** makes this
   return **409** with the impact, so the console can warn with real numbers
   rather than a generic "are you sure".
2. Repeating the request with `confirm: true` applies it — and *withdraws
   that institution's access* as part of the same change: its group and its
   named users come off the client's access policy. A scope that said "not
   you" while the login gate still said "yes" would be a scope in name only.

Widening a scope needs no confirmation and takes nothing away. Adding an
institution does **not** grant its staff access — its own admin still has to
assign the app, which is the point of the two-layer model.

Every change is audited with the actor, the before and after scope, and what
was withdrawn.

post.description:
Give selected employees access to selected applications, creating the
accounts that do not exist yet.

Select from **any** employee in your institution's list, whether or not they
already have an SSO account — sorting them first is this endpoint's job, not
yours:

* **Already has an account** → it is neither recreated nor altered. The
  selected applications are granted on top of what they already have; no
  group move, no password, no set-password email.
* **Has no account** → one is created the usual way: a Keycloak user whose
  username is their email address, a temporary password they are never told,
  a required password reset, membership of the institution's group, and
  Keycloak's own set-password link.

**Validation is per employee, per client.** Each selected application keys
its own user records on one identifier — National ID, phone or email (its
join column, `app/core/join_key.py`) — and employees do not all have all
three. So each (employee, application) pair is decided on its own:

* the field empty → that application is denied, and only that one;
* **already reachable** → skipped and reported as already held, not granted
  again and not refused;
* at least one application to assign → it is assigned; for an employee with
  no account, that is also what makes the account worth creating;
* none qualifies **and no account** → no account, because a login that
  reaches nothing is litter with a password-reset email attached. An
  employee who *has* an account is simply told nothing was added; their
  account is untouched;
* the application has no join column chosen → it denies everyone, rather
  than falling back to the platform's email default and filing records
  under an identifier nobody agreed to.

A missing or malformed email address stops an account being **created** — it
is the username — but does not stop an application being assigned to
somebody who already has one.

Idempotent, and in the way that matters: re-running the same selection
creates nothing, grants nothing, and reports every application as already
held. A batch that half-finished is completed by a re-run.

Scoped. Only employees in the institution you administer resolve, and every
application must be within your client scope — a cross-institution client is
403 for the whole request, because that is a request that should not have
been possible rather than a fact about an employee.

The response is the report: per employee, whether they had an account or got
one, which applications were assigned, which they already held, and which
were refused with the empty field named. Every assignment is audited on its
own with the actor, the target user, the application and the timestamp.
`dry_run: true` produces the identical report and writes nothing.

Items name employees by IPPIS employee number. One with no SSO account is
granted through employee provisioning, which creates the account (needs

and applies its per-app join-key rules — a refusal comes back as that
item's `reason`.

**403, nothing changed**, if any item names an employee outside your
institution or an app outside its scope. Otherwise each item stands alone:

* `applied` — done, and audited (actor, person, app, institution, mode,
  channel, timestamp), every item of the request under one `batch_id`;
* `rejected` / `state_changed` — the cell is no longer what you saw: a grant
  for someone who now has access, a revoke for someone who no longer does.
  Someone else changed it since your page loaded; reload.
* `rejected` / `not_manageable` — your role may view this app but not change
  its access;
* `failed` — Keycloak refused the write for that app.

A grant names the person on the app's access policy (and lifts a standing
revocation of them); a revoke un-names them and/or adds them to the app's
deny-list when they hold it through their institution's group — the group
is never changed.

get.description:
Current state of the realm-wide TOTP switch.

`enforced` is the attribute (unset reads as true); `effective` is whether a
code is actually being asked for, which also needs the realm's browser flow
to be `browser-totp` (`flow_ready`).

put.description:
Set the TOTP mode: `off`, `per_client` or `all`. Super admins only.

`per_client`: a client requires TOTP unless its own setting says otherwise
(unset = required; see PUT /client/clients/{id}/mfa). Takes effect at the
next login, no restart. The first time the mode becomes `all`, every
existing user without an OTP credential is also given CONFIGURE_TOTP (in
the background; audited as `admin.mfa.bulk_enrol`). 409 when the TOTP flow
is not bound yet and the mode is not `off`.

get.description:
Proxy Keycloak's SAML IdP descriptor so SAML SPs can fetch metadata
from the wrapper's stable URL instead of constructing the Keycloak URL.

Get users from the realm with comprehensive filtering options:
    
    **Filter Options:**
    - **client_id**: Get users who have roles for a specific client/portal (e.g., kubaka-web)
    - **agency_id**: Get users belonging to a specific agency/institution
    - **role**: Filter users by specific realm role
    - **search**: Search by username, email, firstName, or lastName
    - **enabled**: Filter by enabled/disabled status
    - **email_verified**: Filter by email verification status
    
    **Pagination:**
    - **page**: Page number (starts at 1)
    - **page_size**: Number of users per page (1-100)
    
    **Use Cases:**
    - Get all users: `GET /users`
    - Get users for kubaka-web portal: `GET /users?client_id=kubaka-web`
    - Get MININFRA employees: `GET /users?agency_id={MININFRA_ID}`
    - Search for users: `GET /users?search=john`
    - Get employees with specific role: `GET /users?role=employee`
    - Combine filters: `GET /users?client_id=kubaka-web&role=employee&page=1`
    
    **Response includes:**
    - Basic user information (id, username, email, names)
    - List of agencies user belongs to
    - Realm roles assigned to user
    - Client roles for each portal

post.description:
Create a fully provisioned user in one atomic operation.
    This endpoint combines:
    1. User creation
    2. Password setting
    3. Group/Agency assignment
    
    **All operations are atomic** - if any step fails, the user is automatically deleted (rollback).
    
    **Required Fields:**
    - username: Unique username
    - email: User's email address
    - firstName: User's first name
    - lastName: User's last name
    - password: Initial password (min 8 characters)
    - group_ids: Array of agency/group IDs to assign user to (min 1)
    
    **Optional Fields:**
    - temporary: Whether password is temporary (default: false)
    - enabled: Whether user is enabled (default: true)
    - emailVerified: Whether email is verified (default: false)
    - attributes: Custom user attributes
    
    **Access Control:** System admins only
    
    **Example:**
    ```json
    {
      "username": "oswaldo.grimaud",
      "email": "oswaldo.grimaud@risa.gov.rw",
      "firstName": "Oswaldo",
      "lastName": "Grimaud",
      "password": "SecurePass123!",
      "temporary": false,
      "group_ids": ["34bd8771-2f95-420e-9fa1-d76a6dde4fa3"],
      "enabled": true,
      "emailVerified": true
    }
    ```
    
    **Response:**
    Returns the created user with full enrichment (agencies, roles, clients).
